\chapter{Greetings and responses}
\label{ch:urdu-greetings}
\hlchaptermodality{1}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can greet someone in Urdu, respond courteously, and close the exchange naturally. I can also write the three shapes inside shukriyā and the letter sīn from memory.}

Complete UR-C01-nahin, the canonical closing checkpoint, and demonstrate the chapter promise: greet someone in Urdu, respond courteously, and close the exchange naturally.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[salām]{\ur{سلام} — hello across a family of languages}

\label{lesson:UR-C01-salam}



\begin{quote}
This is the first Urdu word in this book, and the one you will reach for most. Nothing has to be written today. Look, listen, say it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — notice the direction}
Urdu is written \textbf{right to left}, traditionally in the flowing Nastaliq style. Begin with four letters:

\begin{quote}
\ur{س} \emph{s} · \ur{ل} \emph{l} · \ur{ا} long \emph{ā} · \ur{م} \emph{m} $\to$ \textbf{salām}
\end{quote}

Letters usually connect inside a word. The tall \textbf{\ur{ا}} does not connect onward to the final \textbf{\ur{م}}, creating a visible break. That is enough script for today.

Each of these letters gets a lesson of its own later; their shapes and names here follow \href{https://openbooks.library.northwestern.edu/zerozabar/chapter/the-urdu-alphabet/}{Zero Zabar: the Urdu alphabet}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{salām} is both a greeting and the word “peace.” Urdu received it through the Persian-Arabic literary world. Its consonants \textbf{s-l-m} belong to a Semitic family concerned with peace, safety, and wholeness. Persian \emph{salâm} and Arabic \emph{salām} are the same historical word; Hebrew \emph{shalom} is a relative.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn — use it}
Say \textbf{salām} as a friendly short greeting. You will later extend it into the full conventional exchange. For now the safest reply is the same word back.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item A: \textbf{\ur{سلام}!} — \emph{salām!}
  \item B: \textbf{\ur{سلام}!} — \emph{salām!}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read \textbf{\ur{سلام}} right to left. Which letter carries the long \emph{ā}? \textbf{\ur{ا}}. Now cover the romanization and say \textbf{salām} once, picturing “peace.”
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[shīn, kāf, re]{\ur{ش} \ur{ک} \ur{ر} — three shapes, then stop}

\label{lesson:UR-W01-shukriya-first-three}



\begin{quote}
Urdu runs from right to left. Point to the right-hand edge of your page. Today you will meet only three shapes from the spoken word \emph{shukriyā}. The complete joined word waits for the next lesson.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — recognize three shapes}
Take one shape at a time:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{shape} & \textbf{sound} & \textbf{one thing to notice} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ur{ش}} & \emph{sh} & three dots above \\
\textbf{\ur{ک}} & \emph{k} & a long slash inside the upper shape \\
\textbf{\ur{ر}} & \emph{r} & a simple falling curve \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Read them from right to left once: \textbf{\ur{ش} · \ur{ک} · \ur{ر}} — \emph{sh · k · r}.

\subsection*{Writing — trace before you copy}
Write these out:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item trace \textbf{\ur{ش}} once; pause before adding its three dots
  \item trace \textbf{\ur{ک}} once; notice the separate slash
  \item trace \textbf{\ur{ر}} once; let the curve fall
\end{itemize}

Tracing is enough. Do not join the shapes or write from memory yet.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Point in this order: \emph{sh}, \emph{k}, \emph{r}. Stop after three. The next short lesson adds the final two shapes and only then lets you copy the whole word.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[shukriyā]{\ur{شکریہ} — thank you}

\label{lesson:UR-C01-shukriya}



\begin{quote}
Point to \textbf{\ur{ش} · \ur{ک} · \ur{ر}} and say \emph{sh · k · r}. You traced those three shapes already. Keep your pen down while you meet only two more.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — add two shapes}
Urdu normally omits short-vowel marks. In \textbf{\ur{شکریہ}}, the visible letters guide you, while the vowels complete the learned word:

\begin{quote}
\ur{ش} · \ur{ک} · \ur{ر} · \ur{ی} · \ur{ہ} $\to$ \textbf{shukriyā}
\end{quote}

You already know \textbf{\ur{ش}} \emph{sh}, \textbf{\ur{ک}} \emph{k}, and \textbf{\ur{ر}} \emph{r}. Add \textbf{\ur{ی}} \emph{y/i} and final \textbf{\ur{ہ}}. That is two new shapes, not five. The final vowel is pronounced long \emph{ā} in this familiar expression.

\begin{cousinweb}
The central consonants \textbf{sh-k-r} belong to the Arabic family for gratitude and thanks; Arabic \emph{shukran} is a close comparison. Urdu \textbf{shukriyā} reflects the centuries-long Persian-Arabic layer of its vocabulary — and for all that history it is an ordinary, everyday modern Urdu expression.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{salām} — Hello. You can say it; its letters are still ahead of you, so it is printed here the way you say it.
  \item \textbf{\ur{شکریہ}} — \emph{shukriyā} — Thank you. This one you can already read.
\end{itemize}

Say the second word slowly once, then at a natural pace. Keep \emph{shuk-ri-yā} as three light beats.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} copy \textbf{\ur{شکریہ}} once while looking at the model; do not write it from memory yet
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{shukriyā} once after the pen stops
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two shapes did this lesson add? \textbf{\ur{ی}} and final \textbf{\ur{ہ}}. Greet, then thank: \textbf{salām — shukriyā}. Copying with a model is enough for today.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[jī hā̃]{\ur{جی} \ur{ہاں} — yes, respectfully}

\label{lesson:UR-C01-ji-han}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\ur{شکریہ}} once. Point to its first three shapes, then its final two. Your pen can rest; this lesson is for a spoken respectful answer.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The two words}
The phrase is written right to left, so \textbf{\ur{جی}} is the word on the right:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{جی}} \emph{jī} + \textbf{\ur{ہاں}} \emph{hā̃} $\to$ \textbf{jī hā̃} $\to$ yes
\end{quote}

In \textbf{\ur{جی}}, \textbf{\ur{ج}} gives \emph{j} and \textbf{\ur{ی}} stretches the vowel to \emph{ī}. In \textbf{\ur{ہاں}}, the final sign \textbf{\ur{ں}} marks a nasal vowel: let some air pass through your nose as you say \emph{ā}. It is not a full English \emph{n} at the end.

That sign has a name — \textbf{nūn ghunna} — and you will meet it again.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: respect inside “yes”}]
\textbf{\ur{ہاں}} alone means “yes.” \textbf{\ur{جی}} adds respect and attentive warmth; it can also be used by itself as a polite response. Learning \textbf{jī hā̃} first gives you a safe answer for many situations.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “Do you understand?” — \textbf{\ur{جی} \ur{ہاں۔}} — \emph{jī hā̃.}
  \item “Would you like to continue?” — \textbf{\ur{جی} \ur{ہاں،} \ur{شکریہ۔}} — Yes, thank you.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which mark makes the vowel nasal? Final \textbf{\ur{ں}}. Answer politely: \textbf{jī hā̃}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sīn]{\ur{س} — three teeth, then a bowl, without lifting}

\label{lesson:UR-W01-sin}



\begin{quote}
Point at \textbf{\ur{ش}}, the first shape inside \emph{shukriyā}. Three teeth in a row, a bowl, and three dots floating above.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\ur{س}
\end{quote}

Three small \textbf{teeth} close together — short upward points in a row — and then the line flows straight on into a \textbf{bowl} below the baseline.

Remember which way you are working: the first tooth you draw is the \textbf{rightmost} one.

\textbf{No lift anywhere.} Teeth and bowl are one continuous movement, and letting the pen stop between them is the commonest way a beginner's sīn comes out looking like two letters.

Its name is \textbf{sīn} and it says \textbf{s}.

You have seen this shape before. \textbf{\ur{ش}} \emph{shīn}, from \emph{shukriyā}, is this exact letter wearing three dots above it. Take the dots off and you have \textbf{\ur{س}}. That is the first pair of many: in Urdu a great deal of the alphabet is one skeleton shared by two or three letters, told apart only by dots.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ur{س} — three teeth from the right, flowing into the bowl, one movement
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{s}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which tooth comes first? (The \textbf{rightmost}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nahī̃]{\ur{نہیں} — no, and later “not”}

\label{lesson:UR-C01-nahin}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{jī hā̃, shukriyā} — “yes, thank you.” Now learn the answer that contrasts with \emph{yes}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — recombine known shapes}
You have seen \textbf{\ur{ہ}}, \textbf{\ur{ی}}, and nasal \textbf{\ur{ں}}. Add \textbf{\ur{ن}} \emph{n} at the right:

\begin{quote}
\ur{ن} · \ur{ہ} · \ur{ی} · \ur{ں} $\to$ \textbf{nahī̃}
\end{quote}

Stretch \emph{ī} slightly and nasalize it. The final \textbf{\ur{ں}} does not add a strong separate \emph{n} sound.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one word, two future jobs}]
As a complete answer, \textbf{nahī̃} means “no.” Inside a sentence it commonly means “not.” That second job will matter when the track introduces verbs. Today you only need the complete answer.

Unlike the Persian-Arabic vocabulary that opened this chapter, this word is inherited Indo-Aryan, part of Urdu's own core. Hindi says the same spoken word, \emph{nahī̃}, and writes it in a different script — which you do not need here. The page looks different; the word and its grammar align closely.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{jī hā̃} — yes. Said, not yet read: its first letter is one you have not met.
  \item \textbf{\ur{نہیں}} — \emph{nahī̃} — no. This one you built out of known shapes a moment ago.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does final \textbf{\ur{ں}} do? It nasalizes the vowel. Answer “no”: \textbf{nahī̃}.
\end{tcolorbox}
